subtopic_detail: Deciding which patient with airflow obstruction warrants testing for an inherited protease inhibitor deficiency
stem:
You are the resident in a respiratory clinic. A 43-year-old woman is referred with 2 years of progressive exertional breathlessness and a daily cough productive of clear sputum.

She has never smoked and has worked as a primary school teacher. She has no history of childhood asthma and no occupational dust or fume exposure. Her brother was diagnosed with emphysema at 47 and her father died of liver cirrhosis at 58 with no history of alcohol use.

She takes no regular medicines. On examination the chest is hyperinflated with quiet breath sounds throughout and no wheeze. Spirometry shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 1.52 L (58 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.40 L (94 per cent predicted), ratio 0.45, with a 4 per cent improvement after bronchodilator. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation. High resolution computed tomography of the chest reports panlobular emphysema most marked in the lower zones. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and liver function tests are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Hyperinflated chest with quiet breath sounds throughout, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 1.52 L (58 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.40 L (94 per cent predicted), ratio 0.45, 4 per cent post-bronchodilator improvement. Chest radiograph hyperinflation. High resolution computed tomography: panlobular lower zone emphysema. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin concentration, with phenotyping if the level is reduced
options.rationale: Emphysema in a lifelong non-smoker under 45 with lower zone panlobular distribution and a family history of both early emphysema and unexplained cirrhosis is the classic presentation of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Serum concentration is the appropriate screening test and phenotyping or genotyping follows a low result to characterise the variant. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Serum total immunoglobulin E with specific aeroallergen testing, and skin prick testing if elevated
options.rationale: Allergic assessment supports an asthma diagnosis, and the fixed obstruction with only 4 per cent bronchodilator reversibility and emphysema on imaging argues against that. Testing would be appropriate for variable airflow obstruction with significant bronchodilator response and a compatible history. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Sweat chloride testing, with cystic fibrosis gene panel analysis if the result is elevated
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis produces bronchiectasis with upper lobe predominance, purulent sputum and pancreatic and gastrointestinal features rather than isolated lower zone panlobular emphysema. It would be worth testing for bronchiectasis with recurrent infections and malabsorption. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Serum angiotensin converting enzyme, with tissue biopsy if the level is elevated
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis causes upper zone predominant interstitial change with hilar lymphadenopathy and a restrictive or mixed pattern, not obstructive physiology with panlobular emphysema. It would be considered for bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticulonodular infiltrates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing, with renal biopsy if the titre is elevated
options.rationale: Vasculitis affecting the lung presents with nodules, cavities, haemorrhage or infiltrates alongside renal or upper airway involvement, none of which is present. Testing would be appropriate for haemoptysis with pulmonary infiltrates and an active urinary sediment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is substantially underdiagnosed, with typical delays of many years between first symptoms and recognition, largely because emphysema is assumed to require smoking. The protein is a protease inhibitor produced in the liver that protects alveolar tissue from neutrophil elastase, so deficiency allows unopposed proteolysis in the lower zones where perfusion and neutrophil traffic are greatest, producing the characteristic basal panlobular pattern that contrasts with the upper zone centrilobular emphysema of smoking. The same mutation causes liver disease through accumulation of misfolded protein in hepatocytes, which is why unexplained cirrhosis in a relative is such a useful clue. Testing is recommended for all patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and particularly those presenting young, never-smokers, those with a basal predominant distribution and those with a suggestive family history. Diagnosis changes management: smoking avoidance becomes critical, family members warrant testing and counselling, and augmentation therapy may be considered in selected patients.
key_points: Suspect deficiency in emphysema that is early onset, in a never-smoker, or basal predominant
Panlobular lower zone emphysema contrasts with upper zone centrilobular disease from smoking
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or family is an important associated clue
Serum concentration is the screening test, followed by phenotyping or genotyping
Diagnosis has implications for family screening and counselling as well as for the patient
explanation.pearls: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is an acute phase reactant, so a level measured during an infection or exacerbation can be falsely normal in a deficient patient; recheck when the C-reactive protein has settled.

subtopic_detail: Confirming a workplace cause for adult onset asthma before recommending removal from exposure
stem:
You are the resident in a respiratory clinic. A 34-year-old man is referred with 8 months of cough, chest tightness and wheeze that began 2 years after he started work as a spray painter in a vehicle repair shop.

He reports symptoms build through the working week and are noticeably better on weekends and were absent during a 3 week holiday. He uses a supplied respirator inconsistently. He has never smoked and had no childhood asthma or atopy.

On examination the chest is clear today, having been reviewed on a Monday morning. Spirometry today shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 3.62 L (96 per cent predicted) with a ratio of 0.79 and a 6 per cent bronchodilator response. Chest radiograph is normal. Full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5). He is worried about losing his job and asks whether he really has to leave the trade.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, assessed on a Monday morning
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 3.62 L (96 per cent predicted), ratio 0.79, 6 per cent bronchodilator response. Chest radiograph normal. Eosinophil count 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)
data_table.Occupational: Spray painter for approximately 3 years; symptoms build across the working week, resolve at weekends and during a 3 week holiday; inconsistent respirator use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise immediate permanent removal from spray painting work and commence inhaled corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Removing a worker from their trade has major financial and legal consequences and should follow objective confirmation rather than history alone, which is unreliable in isolation. Immediate removal would be justified once the diagnosis is objectively established, since continued exposure worsens long-term outcome. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

options.text: Arrange serial peak expiratory flow recordings across periods at work and away from work
options.rationale: A single normal spirometry taken after a weekend away from exposure cannot exclude occupational asthma, because airflow obstruction recovers between exposures early in the disease. Serial peak flow diaries across at least 2 weeks at work and 2 weeks away demonstrate the work-related pattern objectively, which is required before advising a change that will end his livelihood. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

options.text: Commence inhaled corticosteroid with a long acting beta agonist and continue current work practices
options.rationale: Treating the inflammation while exposure continues allows progressive airway remodelling and permanent impairment, which is what distinguishes this from ordinary asthma management. Controller therapy is appropriate but only alongside exposure control, not as a substitute for it. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

options.text: Arrange high resolution computed tomography of the chest to assess for an interstitial process
options.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging investigates hypersensitivity pneumonitis or interstitial disease, which cause breathlessness with crackles and restrictive physiology rather than episodic wheeze with normal spirometry. It would be indicated if there were crackles, hypoxaemia or a restrictive pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to common aeroallergens to establish an atopic basis for the symptoms
options.rationale: Common aeroallergen testing does not address workplace sensitisers such as isocyanates, and a negative result would not exclude occupational asthma. Specific immunological testing to the workplace agent, where available, is the relevant investigation rather than a standard environmental panel. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

explanation.summary: Occupational asthma accounts for a meaningful share of adult onset asthma and is important because it is potentially curable if exposure ceases early, while continued exposure leads to fixed airflow obstruction. Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are among the commonest Australian causes, alongside flour, wood dusts, latex and laboratory animal proteins. The history of symptoms improving away from work and on holidays is suggestive but not sufficient, since recall is unreliable and the consequences of a diagnosis are severe for the worker. Serial peak flow monitoring, ideally four or more readings daily across at least 2 weeks working and 2 weeks away, is the accessible objective test, with specific inhalation challenge available only in specialised centres, and timing of assessment matters because spirometry performed after a break from exposure is frequently normal, as happened here. Prognosis depends heavily on the interval between symptom onset and removal from exposure, so investigation should be prompt rather than leisurely.
key_points: Adult onset asthma with symptoms improving away from work should prompt an occupational assessment
Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are a common Australian sensitiser
Normal spirometry after time away from exposure does not exclude the diagnosis
Serial peak flow diaries across periods at and away from work provide objective confirmation
Prognosis depends on how early exposure ceases, so avoid delay in investigating
explanation.pearls: Ask what day of the week the patient is being assessed: a Monday morning clinic after a weekend away from exposure is the least likely time to capture the airflow obstruction that confirms occupational asthma.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: Occupational respiratory disease

subtopic_detail: Bedside manoeuvres separating dynamic outflow obstruction from fixed valvular stenosis
stem:
You are the resident in a cardiology clinic. A 24-year-old man is referred after collapsing while playing football. He describes a few seconds of greying vision as he sprinted, then waking on the ground with bystanders around him.

He has had two similar near-collapses while exercising over the past year, each resolving within a minute of stopping. He has no chest pain at rest and no palpitations. His father died suddenly at 41 while swimming and no autopsy findings were ever discussed with the family.

On examination the pulse is sharp with a rapid upstroke. The apex beat is forceful and undisplaced with a palpable double impulse. There is a harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that does not radiate to the carotids. The murmur becomes louder when he stands from squatting and softer during a sustained handgrip. There is no ejection click. Electrocardiogram shows deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Sharp pulse with rapid upstroke, forceful undisplaced apex with palpable double impulse, harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge without carotid radiation, louder on standing from squatting, softer with sustained handgrip, no ejection click
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: deep narrow Q waves inferolaterally with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Fixed valvular aortic stenosis from a calcified congenitally bicuspid valve
options.rationale: A fixed valvular lesion produces a murmur that softens rather than intensifies on standing, because reduced stroke volume decreases flow across the fixed orifice, and it characteristically radiates to the carotids with a slow rising pulse. The near-pair distinction is that both give a harsh mid-systolic murmur with exertional syncope, but the pulse character and response to manoeuvres are opposite. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Ventricular septal defect with left to right shunting across a perimembranous defect
options.rationale: A septal defect produces a pansystolic rather than mid-systolic murmur and would not generate exertional syncope with a double apical impulse and inferolateral Q waves. It would be the diagnosis for a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a thrill and a normal pulse character. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction from asymmetric septal hypertrophy
options.rationale: A murmur that intensifies with standing from squatting and softens with handgrip indicates dynamic obstruction, because reduced preload and afterload bring the hypertrophied septum and mitral apparatus closer together. The sharp rapid upstroke pulse, double apical impulse, absence of carotid radiation and inferolateral Q waves complete the picture. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse with late systolic regurgitation through a myxomatous valve
options.rationale: Prolapse produces a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur at the apex, and although the click moves earlier on standing there is no click described here. It would be the diagnosis with an audible click and an apical late systolic murmur. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Pulmonary valve stenosis with right ventricular overload and post-stenotic dilatation
options.rationale: Pulmonary stenosis produces an upper left sternal edge murmur with an ejection click and right ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram, not left ventricular hypertrophy with inferolateral Q waves. It would be suggested by right axis deviation and a click varying with respiration. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

explanation.summary: Exertional syncope in a young person with a family history of sudden death is a presentation that demands explanation rather than reassurance, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cardiac cause of sudden death in young athletes. The physical signs follow directly from the physiology: a hypertrophied septum narrows the outflow tract during systole, and anything that reduces ventricular cavity size increases the obstruction. Standing from squatting drops preload and makes the murmur louder, while squatting and sustained handgrip increase preload and afterload respectively and make it quieter, which is the exact reverse of a fixed valvular lesion. The electrocardiogram is abnormal in the great majority of patients and deep narrow Q waves reflect septal hypertrophy rather than infarction. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and quantifies the gradient, after which risk stratification determines whether an implantable defibrillator is indicated, and first-degree relatives require screening because inheritance is autosomal dominant.
key_points: Exertional syncope with a family history of sudden death requires cardiac investigation, not reassurance
Reduced preload increases dynamic obstruction, so standing from squatting makes the murmur louder
Handgrip increases afterload and softens a dynamic murmur while intensifying a regurgitant one
A sharp rapid upstroke pulse without carotid radiation contrasts with the slow rising pulse of valvular stenosis
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so first-degree relatives require screening
explanation.pearls: Deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads of a young patient represent septal hypertrophy rather than prior infarction, and their presence alongside left ventricular hypertrophy should prompt echocardiography before any exercise clearance is given.

subtopic_detail: Obligations and screening after silicosis is identified in an engineered stone benchtop worker
stem:
You are the registrar in a respiratory clinic. A 38-year-old man is referred with 10 months of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has cut and polished engineered stone benchtops in a fabrication workshop for 9 years, frequently dry cutting without water suppression.

He has never smoked. He reports no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats, and no joint pain, rash or dry eyes.

On examination there is no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy and fine inspiratory crackles at both bases. Spirometry shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.68 L (72 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.24 L (70 per cent predicted), ratio 0.83, with a diffusing capacity 62 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography reports multiple small centrilobular and subpleural nodules with an upper zone predominance, with enlarged hilar nodes showing peripheral calcification. Interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis is negative, and antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: No clubbing or lymphadenopathy, fine inspiratory crackles at both bases
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.68 L (72 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.24 L (70 per cent predicted), ratio 0.83, diffusing capacity 62 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography: small centrilobular and subpleural nodules with upper zone predominance, hilar nodes with peripheral calcification. Interferon gamma release assay negative, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at an immunosuppressive dose and continue current work with a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not alter the natural history of silicosis and the fibrosis progresses even after exposure ends, so immunosuppression adds risk without benefit. Steroid therapy would be appropriate for sarcoidosis, which can produce a similar nodular pattern but lacks the exposure history. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Commence antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib and continue current work with a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Antifibrotics are established in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive fibrosing phenotypes, not as primary therapy for silicosis, and continuing exposure would undermine any benefit. Nintedanib would be considered for a progressive fibrosing course after specialist assessment, alongside exposure cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Commence a standard four drug antituberculous regimen and continue current work with a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Silicosis substantially increases tuberculosis risk and screening is mandatory, but the interferon gamma release assay is negative and there are no clinical features of active disease. Treatment would be indicated for a positive screen with active disease, or preventive therapy for latent infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Notify the occupational health authority, remove him from further exposure and screen co-workers
options.rationale: Silicosis is a notifiable occupational disease in Australian jurisdictions and there is no treatment that reverses established fibrosis, so exposure cessation is the only intervention that alters disease trajectory. Notification triggers workplace inspection and screening of co-workers, who share the same exposure and are frequently affected without symptoms. (Source: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

options.text: Arrange surgical lung biopsy to confirm the histological pattern before making any workplace recommendation
options.rationale: The occupational history with a characteristic upper zone nodular pattern and calcified hilar nodes makes this a clinical and radiological diagnosis not requiring tissue. Biopsy would be considered only where imaging is atypical and an alternative diagnosis would change management. (Source: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

explanation.summary: Australia experienced a marked resurgence of silicosis driven by the engineered stone benchtop industry, where the material contains a far higher crystalline silica content than natural stone and dry cutting generates extremely high respirable dust concentrations. The disease has been seen in young workers after unusually short latency, in contrast to the decades-long course of classical silicosis from mining. Diagnosis rests on occupational history with characteristic imaging showing upper zone predominant small nodules, and calcified hilar nodes are a supportive feature. There is no disease-modifying drug therapy, which makes exposure control and early detection the entire strategy, and notification is both a legal duty and the mechanism by which other exposed workers are identified. Associated risks require active surveillance, since tuberculosis, autoimmune connective tissue disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer all occur at increased rates and progression continues for years after exposure ceases.
key_points: Engineered stone has very high crystalline silica content and dry cutting produces extreme dust exposure
Silicosis is notifiable in Australian jurisdictions and notification triggers co-worker screening
No pharmacological therapy alters the disease, so exposure cessation is the primary intervention
Upper zone predominant nodules with calcified hilar nodes are characteristic on imaging
Screen for tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, renal impairment and lung cancer on an ongoing basis
explanation.pearls: Tuberculosis risk is increased several-fold in silicosis and remains elevated for life, so annual screening continues even after the worker has left the industry and regardless of how well the lung disease appears to be behaving.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

subtopic_detail: Separating pericardial constriction from myocardial restriction after mediastinal radiotherapy
stem:
You are the registrar in a cardiology clinic. A 54-year-old woman presents with 8 months of progressive abdominal swelling and ankle oedema. She was treated for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 26 with mediastinal radiotherapy and remains in remission.

She describes breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs but sleeps flat on one pillow. She has had two paracenteses at another hospital, each time being told the fluid was a transudate, and was investigated for liver disease with a normal liver biopsy.

On examination the jugular venous pressure is elevated 8 cm above the sternal angle and rises on inspiration. There is tense ascites, pitting oedema to both knees and a firm non-pulsatile liver edge. Heart sounds are normal with an added early diastolic sound. Echocardiography reports normal left ventricular wall thickness, ejection fraction 58 per cent, normal valve appearances, a respirophasic ventricular septal shift and marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity. Brain natriuretic peptide is 128 ng/L (<100).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated 8 cm above the sternal angle and rising on inspiration, tense ascites, pitting oedema to both knees, firm non-pulsatile liver edge, added early diastolic sound
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography: normal left ventricular wall thickness, ejection fraction 58 per cent, normal valves, respirophasic ventricular septal shift, marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity. Brain natriuretic peptide 128 ng/L (<100)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy from infiltration producing impaired myocardial relaxation and compliance
options.rationale: Infiltrative myocardial disease typically thickens the ventricular walls and produces a markedly elevated natriuretic peptide, whereas the walls are normal here and the peptide is only marginally raised. The near-pair distinction is that both cause right-sided failure with preserved ejection fraction, but respiratory interdependence with septal shift is a pericardial phenomenon absent in myocardial restriction. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

options.text: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension producing ascites and secondary peripheral fluid retention
options.rationale: Hepatic ascites is not accompanied by an elevated jugular venous pressure, and the liver biopsy was normal, so the liver is congested rather than diseased. Cirrhosis would be the diagnosis with a normal venous pressure, stigmata of chronic liver disease and confirmatory histology. (Source: GESA: Ascites)

options.text: Severe tricuspid regurgitation producing systolic venous congestion and secondary hepatic enlargement
options.rationale: Significant tricuspid regurgitation produces a pansystolic murmur, large venous v waves and a pulsatile liver, and the echocardiogram reported normal valves. It would be the diagnosis with those examination findings and regurgitation demonstrated on colour Doppler. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

options.text: Pulmonary arterial hypertension producing right ventricular pressure overload and systemic congestion
options.rationale: Pulmonary hypertension causes right ventricular dilatation and hypertrophy with a raised estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure, none of which is described on the echocardiogram. It would also be expected to cause exertional syncope and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

options.text: Pericardial constriction producing equalisation of diastolic pressures between the cardiac chambers
options.rationale: A rigid pericardium isolates the heart from intrathoracic pressure changes, producing the respirophasic septal shift and exaggerated mitral inflow variation seen here as the ventricles compete for a fixed total volume. A jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration and prior mediastinal radiotherapy, a well recognised cause with a latency of decades, complete the picture. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

explanation.summary: Constrictive pericarditis is one of the most frequently missed causes of right heart failure, and patients commonly accumulate years of gastroenterological investigation for ascites before the venous pressure is examined properly. The physiology is distinctive: a thickened non-compliant pericardium prevents transmission of intrathoracic pressure changes to the cardiac chambers, so inspiration no longer augments right-sided filling and the jugular venous pressure paradoxically rises, and the two ventricles become interdependent within a fixed total volume so that inspiratory right ventricular filling displaces the septum leftward. Distinguishing it from restrictive cardiomyopathy matters enormously because constriction is surgically curable by pericardiectomy while myocardial restriction is not. Helpful discriminators include normal wall thickness, a natriuretic peptide that is normal or only slightly elevated, and respiratory variation in inflow velocities. Prior cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiotherapy and tuberculosis are the leading causes, and radiation-induced constriction may appear decades after treatment.
key_points: A jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration is highly suggestive of constriction
Respirophasic septal shift and exaggerated mitral inflow variation reflect ventricular interdependence
Normal wall thickness with a normal or minimally raised natriuretic peptide favours constriction over restriction
Mediastinal radiotherapy, prior cardiac surgery and tuberculosis are the main causes
Constriction is surgically curable by pericardiectomy, unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy
explanation.pearls: A brain natriuretic peptide that is normal or only marginally elevated in a patient with florid right heart failure argues strongly for constriction, because the normal myocardium is not stretched, whereas infiltrative restriction drives the peptide substantially higher.
